column1: # cases.tsv - the verdict table for harness/shared/guards/never-automatic.sh.
#   rule      the guard_rule id from permissions.yml, or - when expect is allow
#   command   the command string handed to the guard, verbatim
#   why       what this row is here to prove
# harness/scripts/deny-proof.sh runs every row and fails the build on any
# disagreement. It also fails if any never-automatic entry in permissions.yml has a
# guard_rule that no row exercises, which is what stops the table drifting behind
# The allow rows matter as much as the deny rows. A guard that refuses everything
# passes a deny test and makes the harness unusable, so half of this table exists to
# prove the tiers above never-automatic still reach their own rules.
# Rows are data, not shell. Nothing here is executed - the guard is a text
# classifier and deny-proof.sh only ever passes these strings to it as an argument.

column4: why
The plain spelling. If this passes, nothing below matters.
A global option before the subcommand. A harness rule anchored on the first two words misses this one.
Inline config, and the short flag last, so trailing-flag matching has to work too.
Quoted subcommand. --force-with-lease is safer than --force and still rewrites what a colleague holds.
Absolute path and mixed case. Normalisation, not luck.
The refspec form, which carries no force flag at all and is a force-push.
A known over-match, kept deliberately. Writing about a force-push is refused because the guard reads text, not intent. One prompt is the whole cost.
Merging is a human act.
Requesting review spends other people's attention under your name.
Publishing under the project's name.
The same action through the API. The transport does not change the tier.
The target is in the command and it is still not automatic.
A change users can see.
-auto-approve is the exact flag that removes the human this tier exists to keep.
The human's workspace credential. Reading it hands this session their full authority.
Prints a live token into the transcript and every log that captured it.
A private key.
Keychain access. A changed HOME does not isolate the keychain.
Reading harness config through a language runtime rather than cat. Same file, different program, same verdict.

column3: gh pr comment 12 --body "looks good to me"
column4: Arrives as a notification with a human's name on it.
Puts an item on someone's queue.
Rooted outside the repository. Harmless here, refused anyway: the guard cannot tell this path from one that matters.
Deletes ignored files, which is exactly where .env files and unpushed scratch work live.
Throws away local commits that exist in no other copy.
A recursive delete rooted at /.
The most common command in the session must not cost a prompt.

column3: git commit -m "feat: add the never-automatic guard"
column4: Committing locally is auto-allow. Nothing has left the machine.
The load-bearing allow row. A normal push must reach the ask tier and prompt, not be refused here.
Draft pull requests are the ask tier: no reviewer is notified yet.
Reading history.
Without -x this leaves ignored files alone, so it is ordinary tidying.
Tests are the point of the harness.
The repository's own gate.
A long argv with flags, to show the guard is not startled by shape.
Contains "run" and is not a bundle run.
Deleting inside the working tree. The harness's working-directory scope confines the path; this guard does not try to.
Validating is reading. Only deploy, destroy and run are refused.
Listing apps is a read.
Fetching platform documentation over an allowlisted host.
Reading a pull request is not acting on it.
An MCP tool name, not a shell command. A write against a messaging service is a message however the tool is named.
The verb is in the tool name. Replying to a comment notifies whoever wrote it.
A read-only MCP tool from the project's own allowlist.
A workspace write, which belongs to the ask tier and must prompt rather than be refused here.
Reading a channel is a read. Only writes to a messaging service are refused.
Named in the ask tier. The guard must leave it to the permission rules.
